title: How to Make Good Decisions
shortDescription: Making decisions can feel complicated when there is pressure, intense emotions, many opinions, and fear of making a mistake. This eight-day journey will help you develop a biblical framework for making better decisions: remembering who you are, thinking about consequences, listening to counsel, distinguishing emotion from conviction, and learning to move forward without demanding absolute certainty. The goal is not to make perfect decisions, but to grow in wisdom, responsibility, and trust in God.
learning: Recognize how social pressure and the desire for approval can influence decisions
Understand why identity in God should come before important choices
Learn to evaluate decisions in light of biblical principles and real consequences
Distinguish between intense emotions and convictions that endure
Value the counsel of mature people without depending completely on their opinions
Identify when a convenient opportunity is not necessarily a good decision
Learn to decide responsibly even when there is no complete certainty
Develop a more mature way of learning from past mistakes
gains: Greater clarity for making decisions in the midst of pressure or confusion
Less dependence on the approval of friends, social media, or trends
Greater ability to anticipate consequences before acting
More discernment to listen to emotions without automatically obeying them
A more realistic view of opportunities, risks, and limits
More confidence to decide without becoming paralyzed by fear of making a mistake
A more responsible attitude toward mistakes and lessons learned

days.title: Do Not Decide Just to Fit In
days.text:
One of the most powerful forces in many young people's decisions is the need to belong. It can show up in friendships, relationships, studies, social media, parties, or even in the way you speak. Sometimes we know something is not good for us, but we are afraid of being left out.

The Bible warns about the fear of people because it can become a trap. Paul also asks whether he is seeking to please people or God. That does not mean living with contempt for what others think, but avoiding letting other people's approval rule decisions that affect your character and future.

A good decision can feel uncomfortable when it goes against the majority. But fitting in for a moment is not always worth the cost of betraying your convictions. Maturity begins when you learn to endure some discomfort without abandoning what you know is right.
days.internalize: Complete this sentence: “If no one were going to judge or praise me, I would probably choose…”. Notice how much other people's opinions influence your answer.
days.prayer: Lord, give me firmness so I do not live seeking approval at any cost. Help me listen to counsel without becoming a slave to other people's opinions, and help me choose what honors your truth. Amen.
days.action: Identify a recent decision where you felt pressure to fit in. Write down what you would have chosen if you had not been afraid of disappointing someone.

days.title: Remember Who You Are Before You Choose
days.text:
Many decisions are born from questions of identity. We look for a relationship to feel valuable, accept something to prove that we are capable, or imitate others because we still do not know clearly who we want to be.

The Bible places identity in God before any achievement or approval. Peter speaks of a people called by God. Ephesians reminds us that we are his workmanship. That security changes the starting point of a decision.

When you know that your worth does not depend on a response, a relationship, or a result, you can choose with greater freedom. You no longer need to use every decision to prove something about yourself. You can ask what is wise, healthy, and consistent with the person God is forming.
days.internalize: Before an important decision, say: “I do not need this choice to prove how much I am worth. My worth is not at stake.”
days.prayer: Father, establish my identity in You. Free me from making decisions only to feel important, accepted, or enough. Teach me to choose from the security of knowing that I belong to You. Amen.
days.action: Write down a decision you are considering and answer: “Am I trying to resolve an insecurity about who I am through this choice?”

days.title: A Good Decision Needs More Than Good Intentions
days.text:
It is possible to want something good and still make a poor decision about how to pursue it. Good intentions do not replace prudence. A relationship may seem exciting, a purchase may feel deserved, or an opportunity may sound perfect, but every decision needs to be evaluated.

Jesus spoke about counting the cost before building. Proverbs contrasts the naive person, who believes everything, with the one who carefully considers their steps. Wisdom asks about consequences before they arrive.

Thinking before acting does not make you cold or fearful. It helps you recognize what a decision may require from your time, money, emotions, relationships, or future. A good choice is not only the one you like now, but the one you can responsibly sustain afterward.
days.internalize: Use four questions: “What do I gain? What do I lose? What risk am I taking? What consequence might appear later?”
days.prayer: God, give me prudence so I do not confuse enthusiasm with wisdom. Help me consider consequences and choose responsibly, not only with good intentions. Amen.
days.action: Take one pending decision and answer the four questions from today's exercise in writing before moving forward.

days.title: Your Emotions Matter, but They Do Not Have to Rule
days.text:
Emotions can give you valuable information. Fear can point to risk, sadness can reveal loss, and joy can indicate something you value. The problem appears when a temporary emotion becomes the only reason for deciding.

The psalmist speaks to himself when he is discouraged. He does not ignore what he feels, but neither does he allow that state to define all of reality. Proverbs invites us to guard the heart because life flows from it.

A good decision listens to emotion and then examines it. If you are very angry, euphoric, hurt, or desperate, you may need to wait before responding. Some decisions improve greatly after sleeping, praying, and allowing the intensity to settle.
days.internalize: Name the main emotion accompanying your decision and finish this sentence: “I feel this, but I still need to evaluate…”.
days.prayer: Lord, thank You that I can feel deeply. Give me self-control so I do not react impulsively and wisdom to listen to my emotions without allowing them to govern every choice. Amen.
days.action: If a decision is not urgent and you are emotionally overwhelmed, postpone your response until tomorrow. Then review whether the same option still seems wise.

days.title: Learn to Ask for Advice Without Handing Your Life Over to Others
days.text:
Making decisions completely on your own can look like independence, but many times it leaves us trapped in our blind spots. A mature person may notice something we are not seeing.

The Bible values counsel. Jethro helped Moses recognize that his way of working was not sustainable. Proverbs teaches that walking with the wise produces wisdom. However, listening to advice does not mean allowing others to decide for you.

You need to learn to distinguish between someone who helps you think and someone who tries to control you. Good counsel asks questions, points out risks, brings experience, and respects your responsibility. The final decision still requires prayer, reflection, and personal maturity.
days.internalize: A good adviser does not need to live your life for you; they help you see more clearly the life that you will have to live.
days.prayer: Father, surround me with wise and sincere people. Give me humility to listen and maturity to take responsibility for my own decisions. Amen.
days.action: Talk with a mature person about an important decision. Instead of asking, “What should I do?” ask, “What risk or blind spot do you think I am not seeing?”

days.title: Not Every Opportunity Deserves a Yes
days.text:
An opportunity can be possible, attractive, and even permissible, and still not be beneficial. Paul acknowledges that not everything that is lawful builds up. That distinction is very important as more options begin to appear in life.

You may have the opportunity to enter a relationship, accept a job, participate in an activity, or spend money on something you want. The question is not only, “Can I?” but, “What effect will this have on me?”

A good decision considers whether the opportunity strengthens or weakens your priorities. Some options consume more than they offer. Others arrive at the wrong time. Saying no can also be a wise decision, even when no one could accuse you of doing something wrong.
days.internalize: Add a new question to your decisions: “Even if I can do it, is it good for me and does it help me grow?”
days.prayer: Lord, give me discernment so I do not say yes to everything that appears. Help me recognize which opportunities contribute to my growth and which may pull me away from what truly matters. Amen.
days.action: Make a list of your three main priorities in this season. Evaluate one current opportunity by asking whether it strengthens or competes with them.

days.title: You Do Not Need Complete Certainty to Decide
days.text:
The fear of making a mistake can paralyze you. We want to be one hundred percent sure before choosing a career, an opportunity, a relationship, or a change. But many important decisions come without complete guarantees.

James invites us to ask for wisdom. Proverbs reminds us that we make plans while God directs our steps. Walking by faith means accepting that we cannot control every outcome.

After seeking biblical principles, considering consequences, listening to counsel, and reviewing your motives, uncertainty may still remain. That does not mean you must stay still. You can choose the option that seems wisest with the information available and remain humble enough to adjust if new information appears.

Maturing also means learning that a responsible decision does not always feel completely certain.
days.internalize: The goal is not to obtain an impossible guarantee, but to reach enough clarity to act responsibly.
days.prayer: God, give me wisdom to decide and courage to move forward when I have already done what is mine to do. Help me trust that You can direct and correct my steps. Amen.
days.action: Identify a decision you have delayed because you are looking for absolute certainty. Define what reasonable information you still need and what part you will simply have to take on with faith.

days.title: A Bad Decision Does Not Have to Define Your Future
days.text:
Learning to make good decisions also means accepting that sometimes you will get it wrong. You may ignore advice, act impulsively, or discover later that an option was not as good as it seemed. Mistakes are part of the process of maturity, but they do not have to become your identity.

The Bible presents a path of confession, learning, and moving forward. Proverbs speaks of the righteous person rising again. John reminds us of the possibility of forgiveness. Paul refuses to remain trapped in what lies behind.

A bad decision can have real consequences and may require repair. But punishing yourself indefinitely does not change the past. The more mature response is to acknowledge it, correct what you can, learn, and adjust your criteria for the future.

The goal of this plan is not to turn you into someone who never fails, but into someone who makes decisions with increasing wisdom and responds better when mistakes happen.
days.internalize: Close this journey with this conviction: “I can learn from a wrong decision without allowing it to become the definition of my whole life.”
days.prayer: Father, give me humility to recognize my mistakes and grace not to remain trapped in them. Teach me to learn, repair, and keep growing in wisdom. Amen.
days.action: Think of a past decision you learned from. Write down what different criterion you would use today and turn it into a practical rule for your future decisions.
